💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that malika Oubzou is sitting on a red and blue handwoven rug on the floor of her childhood home in Tamda Noumercid, a small village near Azilal in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains.
  • Soon enough, more food comes out: a steaming clay pot of tajine maazi (goat tagine) with potatoes and carrots, fresh tomato salad, and fluffy Tafarnout bread, still warm from the clay oven.
  • Malika Oubzou greets her neighbors at the door of her home in Azilal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that malika Oubzou is sitting on a red and blue handwoven rug on the floor of her childhood home in Tamda Noumercid, a small village near Azilal in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains. The 36-year-old weaving artisan is enjoying a glass of milk and a plump, juicy date from a large plate she’s set out for guests—myself among them—when she looks up to see even more people arriving. To accommodate the fresh visitors, she finishes her milk, leaves the room, and returns with a low table. Then another. And another after that.

Soon enough, more food comes out: a steaming clay pot of tajine maazi (goat tagine) with potatoes and carrots, fresh tomato salad, and fluffy Tafarnout bread, still warm from the clay oven. Malika shifts the tables around to make room for the additional food, and her brother, Mohammed, rearranges the pillows that line the rug-filled floors of the space. It continues like this for the next couple of hours: A table appears here, a pillow moves there. Food comes in and food goes out. The only thing that stays put? The rugs themselves.

Malika Oubzou greets her neighbors at the door of her home in Azilal. In Morocco, Friday is celebrated as "Couscous Day," a cherished tradition where families gather for a communal lunch, usually after the weekly congregational prayer.

Recent findings suggest that “In a typical rural Moroccan household, everything is mobile except the rugs,” Jihane Lahbibi, the Moroccan co-founder of the Moroccan rug brand Casa Amar, tells me as we dunk our Tafarnout into the tagine juices. “The pillows, tables, mattresses…they are all roving. But the rugs are the constant. Symbolically, they are the pillars. They anchor the room. They are the room.” In fact, as Malika echoes later through a translator, rugs are the most sacred part of the home. “When you welcome guests,” she says, “the rug is everything.”.

It has been revealed that malika was the first weaver Jihane and her Italian husband Matteo met when they began looking for artisans to make custom rugs for Casa Amar back in 2021. Today, they partner with women in five communities across Morocco to create and source rugs for clients across the world, and were even part of Milan Design Week last year. As interest in Moroccan craftsmanship and design continues to soar, I’ve come to spend some time with a few of the artisans Jihane and Matteo work with to learn more about the Amazigh weaving culture behind the craft.

This scene with the roving tables is a very good start. It’s impossible to miss the deep significance of rugs in everyday Moroccan life once you experience their starring role in every room, after all. But as the days go by, I realize rugs have taken on even more meaning in recent decades, too: They’ve become a way to keep Amazigh culture alive in the face of modernization.

Recent findings suggest that “Younger generations aren’t making as many rugs these days, so when the older women weavers eventually die, the younger ones won’t know how to make them—and that makes me really, really sad,” Malika tells me after we’ve finished our tagine and have moved on to mint tea and a bowl of grapes for dessert. “So now, when I’m weaving, I think about my culture. I also think about the satisfaction of making something good, and the money I will get from making it. All of those things are key. But rugs are objects that last, and because they last, they are one of the best ways to preserve the culture.”.

Industry observers note that like most Indigenous traditions around the world, Moroccan rug weaving dates back thousands of years. Amazigh women (also known as Berber) in the Atlas Mountains originally crafted handknotted rugs from local sheep’s wool to protect themselves and their families from the elements: harsh sun during the day, and freezing mountain temperatures at night. Over time, rug weaving morphed into an art form as well, one filled with all sorts of storytelling and symbolism. Some rug patterns represent universal emotions like love and hope, while others are more like talismans, meant to protect against evil and infertility. No matter the pattern, though, the weaving tradition itself has never been written down anywhere. It’s passed down from mother to daughter simply by watching.

Sources indicate that nejma Oubzou prepares freshly harvested dwarf palm by cutting the thorns off and separating the fan-like leaves in order to dry them out. The fibers are used to create woven items such as baskets, mats, and home decor.

“Amazigh women know how to make rugs the same way many other people around the world know how to make bread…it’s just a part of the culture from a very young age,” Jihane, who grew up in Casablanca, tells me one afternoon as we’re driving through the mountains. “It’s not like someone sits you down on the loom and says, ‘This is how you do it.’ It’s just that you learn the same way you learn how to walk: No one tells you, you just learn it by seeing.” When she started Casa Amar in 2021 after leaving her job as a business lawyer, she used to ask the artisans she met when, exactly, they learned to weave for the first time. But now she’s come to understand that seeking out that information was always a fool’s errand. “I realize now that it was never so specific,” she reflects. “It was always: They’re around, they see, and they try.”.

Industry observers note that that’s exactly what happened with Malika. She wove her first rug at age 15 after years of watching her mom weave, and then watching her weave some more. But that first rug she ultimately created wasn’t just a result of growing up around looms; it was a way for her to care for her own mind. When she was 10, her older brother asked her to drop out of school. Their sister had just gotten married, their parents worked outside the home in agriculture, and he and his younger brother wanted to stay in school—so he decided Malika would be the one to stay home and handle the household chores. Weaving became her creative outlet as a result. “What happened was that after I finished my household work, I had this emptiness that I wanted to fill, and weaving was how I filled it,” she tells me. “I didn’t go to school and I didn’t work, so weaving was how I took care of my brain. I used it to fill a void.”.

Today, Malika continues to weave to fulfill her creative dreams, and to make money by doing so. She works independently in the home, not as part of one of the thousands of weaving cooperatives scattered throughout Morocco. When she’s weaving a custom rug for Casa Amar, she follows the design given to her by their clients. But when she’s weaving just for herself or her family (which is increasingly rare due to her growing amount of paid work), her patterns are instinctive and intuitive, usually based on how she is feeling in the moment. “There’s no particular reasoning behind so many of my designs; it’s just what I like and what my mind tells me to do,” she explains. “It’s a very free process. It’s not like if you have green, you have to put yellow. You can do whatever you want. It’s all in the mind when you’re making a rug for yourself.”.

Recent findings suggest that but aside from earning a living and expressing her creativity, there’s a third reason Malika weaves: a desire to preserve her craft in the face of modernization. This is where things get slightly complicated because, in some ways, the tradition is thriving. As any design aficionado knows, the allure of Moroccan textiles is increasingly global and well-documented, everywhere from Instagram to the pages of this very magazine. According to the international research firm 6W, the Moroccan rug market is projected to reach $485 million in the US by 2032, up from $371 million in 2025.

Industry observers note that every step of the wool preparation process is done by hand. After the wool is sheared from the animal, the artisans wash, brush, and spin it into yarn.

Sources indicate that latest York-based interior designer Sarah Lederman believes this uptick in interest could be a response to, take a guess, AI. “People are craving more handmade items in their homes now because they’re the opposite of uniform,” she says, “and Moroccan rugs bear the mark of the person who made them.” They’re a reminder, in other words, of what it means to be human.

Recent findings suggest that khadija Rhandouss in the carpet section of the weekly souk in Khmisset. Rhandouss is a local businesswoman who trades in Moroccan rugs. Every Tuesday she attends the weekly souk in Khmisset where all the best rug deals happen before sunrise.

At the same time, there are threats to the longevity of traditional rugmaking. For one thing, as Malika mentioned at multiple points throughout my visit, fewer young women are actually learning the traditional weaving techniques required to make remarked rugs. The work is time-consuming, after all, and the money isn’t always great. And now that there are more profitable career options available elsewhere, many younger women are choosing to leave their villages in the mountains, making weaving less of an obvious path than it once was.

Nejma Oubzou spins wool into yarn at her home in the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.

In a recent development, that’s not to mention the modern technology that has changed the game even more. In the early 2000s, some Moroccan small producers started to buy machines from China that allowed them to process bad-quality wool (known locally as “dead wool”) to make carpets. While starting a upcoming rug used to begin with cutting pure wool from sheep, these machines—which are still used by many today—make it easy to cut out that step entirely. This eliminates a huge and significant part of the process. “A lot of people think that making a carpet is just about weaving on a loom, but actually, making the raw material—i.e., transforming it from sheep to the wool that allows you to start weaving—is just as important,” Ibrahim Noubl, a longtime Moroccan rug dealer, told me in Marrakech at the beginning of my trip. He owns Soufny Art Gallery on the edge of the medina, and often collaborates with the beloved, art-filled hotel El Fenn just a two-minute walk down the road. “In Morocco, we are very sentimental people. We believe in lots of non-material ideas, like the thought that wool is blessed,” he explained. “When blessed wool is inside your home, it will bring you comfort and joy—but all of that disappears when it’s not alive in the first place.”.

Mimouna Fadil attaches the wool to a wooden plank to start a newly introduced rug at her home in Khmisset.

Artisans, particularly from the Amazigh communities, hand-dye the wool using traditional techniques, often boiling it with ingredients to create long-lasting, eco-friendly colors. Red wool in Moroccan rug making is traditionally achieved using natural dyes derived from plants, minerals, and insects to produce vibrant, lasting colors. Earthy reds often come from henna or madder root, while brighter shades are created with pomegranate peels or cochineal insects.

With that in mind, vintage rugs are one of the best bets for high-quality wool, Ibrahim advises, because the product has already survived a few decades—so you know the wool is good. (Carpets made from “dead wool” often start to smell after a few years.) But to keep the ancient traditions alive in a competitive marketplace, companies like Casa Amar, Salam Hello, and the ever-popular Beni Rugs also sell new rugs and put traditional, sustainable craftsmanship front and center. Not only do they use high-grade natural wool (no “dead wool” to be found here), but they also work directly with artisans like Malika, helping provide an income that allows them to continue their traditional and beloved craft.

It has been revealed that nejma Oubzou, mother of Malika, in her bedroom in her home in the Atlas Mountains. Her name means “stars.”.

Many of the artisans even pray before they sit down at the loom because it’s such a sacred act. They start with the Arabic phrase “Bismillah,” which means “in the name of God,” then follow it up with a prayer for peace and serenity during their time on the loom, often including phrases like nsaliw l mensej f salam ou l hna: “We started with peace; may we finish with peace.” After all, as Jihane tells me at various points over the course of our week together, a rug can be both sacred and a source of income. The two are not mutually exclusive. “To buyers, rugs may be just random objects, but people pray before making them, even for people they don’t know,” she says one Friday over Friday couscous, a longtime weekly tradition in Morocco. “I never want to romanticize weaving, because at the end of the day, artisans make the rugs to survive. But both can be true. Just because you have to earn money doesn’t mean you don’t make it respectfully the way your elders did it. It’s something you do with dignity and pride…something to carry the legacy.”.

It has been revealed that for the last leg of my Morocco trip, Jihane takes me to Khemisset, a small market town about an hour’s drive inland from the capital Rabat, where she lives with Matteo and their two (adorable) young sons. Khemisset is known for its surrounding countryside—think rolling wheat fields, fragrant eucalyptus trees, and grazing sheep—plus its Amazigh weaving traditions, particularly its regionally specific palm mats. Not many artisans make these mats anymore except those in the Khemisset countryside and a few others scattered throughout the Atlas Mountains, and they are sadly going extinct as a result—so I wanted to see them before it’s too late. Jihane and Matteo are also trying to help preserve the mats by spreading the word to their customers. “It’s simple: If people know about them and buy them, artisans will keep making them,” she tells me in the car on the drive from Rabat.

It has been revealed that unlike handknotted rugs, these palm mats are woven from dried palm leaves (not wool) and embroidered with colorful wool patterns on top. They typically cost much less than wool rugs because the raw material is cheaper, but they’re equally difficult to make—and a bit harder on the hands. The leaves tend to dry out during the day, even after the artisans boil them for softness and place them in sachets. As a result, the six women I meet—all of whom collaborate with Jihane and Matteo—often weave late into the night when it’s cooler, or in the morning before the sun becomes too strong. Despite these challenging conditions, they love what they do and are determined to keep the craft alive. (Not entirely unrelated, they are also determined to stuff me and Jihane with more dates, milk, Tafarnout bread, olive oil, and honey—the welcome spread of choice throughout our journey.).

Nora Rhandouss, Khadija Rhandouss, and Jihane share mint tea in Khadija’s salon in Khmisset.

Recent findings suggest that “The techniques to make these mats are very old and very ancestral,” 60-year-old Fatiha Amalou, one of the artisans, tells me as we snack on a bowl of particularly glistening dates. We are sitting on a green and white patterned rug on the floor of another artisan’s house, where we’ve all gathered to chat. Not surprisingly, we’re also circled around a low table that, wouldn’t you know, magically appeared when we arrived. “The mats are so sacred that back in the old days, when people would die, we would wrap them up in them to take them away for burial,” Fatiha continues. “They were like a cape.”.

Industry observers note that today, she is dedicated to preserving that sacred weaving tradition. But she also cares deeply about the craftsmanship itself. “Of course I want the legacy to continue; everyone wants the legacy to continue,” she tells me. “But really, perhaps more than anything else, I want to make something that makes me proud. We always say: If you make a good thing, it means you have a good head.” Another artisan, 51-year-old Khadija Rhandouss, nods in agreement. “When I make something good, I feel at peace,” she notes. I tell them all that, as a bit of a perfectionist myself, I can relate to that sentiment wholeheartedly. Fatiha just laughs and smiles. “Yes, weaving is what we need to do to make money,” she says, “but it’s also part of what we do to feel good. It’s part of who we are.”.

A New Azzedine Alaïa Retrospective Goes Beyond the Bandage Dress

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1489 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the bandage dress.
  • Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.
  • It has been revealed that born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the bandage dress. The zipper dress. The perforated leather. The jersey hoods. The peplummed chemises. Azzedine Alaïa’s designs may not look so radical now, but almost 50 years ago, he changed the collective tide of fashion. The bandage dress is perhaps the most pervasive bit of his legacy, and it is emblematic of how the late French-Tunisian designer ushered in a new body-conscious silhouette in the ’80s, one made possible by technological innovations in materials that sculpted without any rigid, waist-cinching structure.

Alaïa’s designs “were completely shocking” to the public at the time, recounts Laura Camerlengo, curator in charge of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. She has spent the past four years developing a new exhibition titled “Azzedine Alaïa: Sculpting Fashion,” the first major U.S. retrospective dedicated to the work of the famed couturier. It opened November 21.

It has been revealed that born in 1935 in Tunis, Alaïa first trained as a sculptor, a background evident in his body of work. In 1956, he decamped to Paris to pursue fashion full-time. After a brief internship at the house of Christian Dior, he worked under Guy Laroche for less than two years before taking on his own private clients, then launching his own atelier in the late ’70s. From there, he built the house we know today. His obsession with construction and material innovation allowed him to both celebrate and liberate the female form. He passed away in late 2017 at the age of 82.

Camerlengo first encountered Alaïa’s work as an assistant on the “Patrick Kelly Runway of Love” exhibition that the Philadelphia Museum of Art organized in 2014. “I was intrigued by how many of the new designers in Paris at this time were being supported by US consumers and retailers,” she says. After ascending to her new position in San Francisco years later, she cold-emailed Olivier Saillard, director of the Azzedine Alaïa Foundation in Paris. He was intrigued, and the two began working together on the exhibition almost immediately.

Sources indicate that the exhibition focuses on 80 garments from across Alaïa’s celebrated career, divided over a series of archetypes—the bandage dresses, sculptures and shapes, black and white, silhouettes and suiting, and construction and craftsmanship—to explore how his design aesthetic evolved. Interspersed are designs worn by devotees like Tina Turner, Grace Jones, and Rihanna. One final gallery highlights his personal collections of the work of designers he most admired, like Christian Dior and Charles James.

Ahead, Camerlengo speaks to Bazaar about curating the upcoming exhibition, contextualizing Alaïa’s work in today’s fashion landscape, and his enduring legacy.

It has been revealed that the exhibition is not chronological. We look at a series of Alaïa’s archetypes like the bandage dress to explore how his design aesthetic evolved over the course of his career. He often himself said that he didn’t want to conform to seasonal trends; he was more interested in the evolution of his designs. And so the gallery highlights a mix of objects dating from the 1980s to his final collection in 2017, and they’re largely grouped by type.

When you come in, you are greeted by Grace Jones, as we say, and the seminal purple hooded bandage dress from the fashion Oscars [a French event held in 1985]. As you move through, you’ll see a selection of the zipper dresses, the chiffon gowns, and other works that tie into some of the other themes. In each space, we mix the time periods. And that was something Alaïa himself often said. [He had a running joke that he didn’t know his own age.] He often said he was “as old as the pharaohs.” Basically, time was a construct for him.

That’s a great word for it. We could think of the popularity of the Japanese fashion designers who obscured women’s bodies with their voluminous styles. We could think of the suiting of the period. The 1970s is this period of workplace equality. Women are wearing suits in the style of masculine dress, but that also means they're obscuring their bodies. And then we can think of pop culture. I always think of Diane Keaton’s Annie Hall in 1977.

It has been revealed that some of the individuals I interviewed for my catalog text who were retailers in San Francisco at the time described Alaïa's designs as being like a whiplash. It was a complete 180 from the styles that they had gotten used to over the past decade, which also includes the rise of T-shirts and jeans for women as a mode of dress.

Industry observers note that so here you have these very sexy, very form-fitting clothes. And part of the Alaïa aesthetic, as I see it, is the reclamation of the gaze. Rather than women being passively looked at—usually by men—they are instead commanding their own agency. As you remarked, it was completely earth-shattering and very shocking at the time.

It has been revealed that azzedine Alaïa was one of the few couturiers who could work completely by the methods of tailoring and by draping, start to finish, from the initial concept to the final product. I did not fully appreciate his tailoring and the suits he constructed beforehand. We have a selection of them in a gallery of the exhibition, and their construction is absolutely incredible. The way they fit the body, the way they uplift and empower women through cloth—again, very antithetical to what we saw in the decades prior in the 1970s. These are very form-fitting, tailored at the waist, but they have soft feminine touches as well that give you this interesting mix of femininity and strength at the same time.

According to recent reports, very notable. We talk in the first gallery about how women, speaking generally, were the architects of his life. He learned to sew from his sister, who was working for a seamstress. He was encouraged by a local midwife in Tunisia to go to school at the Institute of Fine Arts. She helped him forge his papers to read 16—he was only 15 at the time. He learned his skills, not in formal training, but from women in Tunisia.

According to recent reports, and then his early work was supported by a lot of leading figures of international society, including various Rothschilds, the French performer Arletty, the Swedish American actress Greta Garbo, and that's all before he even started to work formally under his own label in the 1980s. Of course, in the 1980s, he adopts Naomi Campbell, who becomes his protégé. He has close relationships with Grace Jones and Tina Turner. They were hugely important to him. In the exhibition, the clear invisible mounts that we use are actually based on the body of Naomi Campbell.

Industry observers note that probably the Grace Jones bandage dress from the fashion Oscars in 1985. Not only is it the progression of the bandage dress style that he experiments with throughout the course of the 1980s, but it represents a key moment in his career where he receives two very high accolades as part of the fashion Oscars and he’s recognized for his genius.

Industry observers note that as far as the designs themselves, I think we would consider the bandage dress, for example, an iconic symbol of late 20th- and 21st-century fashion developed by Azzedine Alaïa, but of course iterated upon extensively. We've seen surges and resurgences in its popularity ever since.

And then as far as the landscape of the broader fashion system, Alaïa was someone who really eschewed seasonal calendars and trends. He was unconcerned with making things for the market. He often wanted to just produce clothes and share them when he felt they were ready. So I think his method of working foreshadows some of the conversations we’re having now about the overproduction of fashion and the overconsumption of fashion, even the detrimental environmental impacts that we see connected to it. He was really a forerunner, in a sense, to question the fashion system.

In a recent development, you can see how he really studied the construction of other garments and then adapted it in his own way in his designs. For example, he admired the work of Charles James, the great American fashion designer who was able to manipulate fabric to achieve weightless volume. And you see in Alaïa's own collections as he continues in his career, he does radial tucks and pleating to also get a certain amount of weightless volume in some of his gowns, very much in the spirit of James.

It has been revealed that I hope our visitors appreciate the artistry of his work, first and foremost, and also the importance of handcraftsmanship. We are increasingly in an age of technology, especially with the rise of AI. What he created by his own hand is something that we can really marvel at.

Latest Update: I Tested Peloton's New, More Affordable Folding Treadmill

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gq

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand.
  • Sources indicate that nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018.
  • According to recent reports, the latest Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in my mind and, I think the minds of many others, Peloton has always been a stationary bike brand. The Bike, after all, was its first product, turning the Peloton name into a catch-all term for at-home cycling that we now hear everywhere, from broadcasts of the Tour de France and Giro d'Italia to television sitcoms. (A running gag online is that Peloton's upscale, soothing video workout content is worlds away from The Office's Dwight Schrute leading a group of stationary riders off an imaginary cliff.).

Sources indicate that nevertheless, Peloton actually has been making treadmills since 2018. The first Tread delivered the same proposition as the Bike: premium hardware that looks good enough to bring out of the basement, as well as access to interactive, instructor-led runs and HIIT classes on a significant, immersive screen. Over the years, Peloton has brought improvements to that first Tread: larger screens, voice controls, AI-informed movement tracking for form analysis and coaching.

According to recent reports, the latest Tread Flex, however, heads in a slightly different direction. It has a simpler belt, simpler speakers, a smaller screen. It's $1,300 cheaper than the next step up, and $4,500 cheaper (!) than Peloton's slat belt-equipped Tread+ Vision. Its affordability isn't even its main selling point, however, because the Tread Flex has a nifty final trick: it folds up to save space.

Could these space and money-saving tactics make the Tread as popular as the Bike? Well, I run nearly every day, and ever since a tester Tread Flex showed up at my door, I've been doing it indoors much more frequently. In my experience, here's what makes Peloton's latest worth considering.

Treadmills tend to have a problem that stationary bikes don't: the nicer they get, the bigger they get. Premium models have larger motors and roomier running platforms. In short, they're heavy. (The Tread+ Vision is a hefty 460 pounds.) The Tread Flex is 170 pounds less, and that's crucial to its ability to fold up, because that feature wouldn't be much of a selling point if it felt like adding a power clean to the end of every run.

In reality, stowing the Tread Flex is quite easy. You just lift up the running deck from the end and push it forward until a hydraulic cylinder locks into place. There's a pin clip to lock it. To drop it down, you push forward on the deck and then on the hydraulic support, then walk it back. At about 45 degrees, the hydraulics take over completely; you can go put on your running shoes while a gentle thump lets you know the deck is back on the ground.

Sources indicate that folding up the Tread Flex drops its area from about 16.5 square feet to half that. (The Tread+ Vision is around 19.25.) Just as importantly, I've discovered, is that lifting the deck brings the machine up onto a set of locking wheels. I've kept mine in a designated corner, but it's so easy to move that it wouldn't be much hassle to wheel it out and lower it for every workout, if your space required it. Get your cardio out of the way, then get your cardio out of the way.

Okay, so folding and moving a treadmill might be a pain if you're using it every day. But I suspect if you're running that often, you're doing some of it outside. I live less than an hour away from the Canadian border, and run on roads and trails five or six times a week all year round. Good layers get you pretty far, and there's a reason why run clubs continue to boom while SoulCycle-adjacent Mile High Run Club closed all its studios this year.

In a recent development, treadmills are for something else. They're for a warm-up prior to lifting, or for bootcamp-style HIIT workouts that combine sprinting intervals with weight intervals. The prioritization value of time spent doing these doesn't seem to align with the space investment a treadmill requires if you don't have a pool house or major garage. (I have a sun porch-slash-mudroom where I keep firewood and ski boots in the winter and a napping couch in the summer.).

This is how, I think, the Tread Flex makes the ultimate proposition as the ideal home treadmill. A treadmill doesn't replace a usual running routine; it adds to it. On Monday I do my usual seven miles down the road and back on the river trails; on Tuesday I let Andy Speer kick my ass with sprints and kickstand deadlifts. (And, sure, when it's -10° and blowing in late January, I might run inside, now that I have the option.).

Sources indicate that none of the above would matter as much if it came at the cost of quality. I've run on hotel treadmills that sound like your grandma's washing machine and feel similar to how they look, i.e., stomping around on hollow plastic. The Tread Flex may not have the cushioned slat belt the Tread+ Vision has, but it's definitely not that.

Industry observers note that what it does have is a spec that's right in line with top-notch treadmills. Its max speed is 12.5 miles per hour (a 4:48 mile, in runner's units), a 12.5% max incline grade (but no decline), and a 20-inch by 59-inch running surface that, though not cushioned, feels good to run on. The swiveling screen is nice and substantial at 21.5 inches, with HD resolution and a touchscreen interface. I particularly like how adjusting speed and incline is done with rolling knobs, which feel much better—and more natural—to engage with than buttons when you're gasping at threshold pace.

On top of that is Peloton's interactive experience: You can take live classes where you can pit yourself against others and get kudos from the instructor. The pre-recorded catalogue includes thousands of classes for yoga, Pilates, and meditation, in addition to strength and the running, cycling, and rowing the company makes machines for.

Industry observers note that the Tread Flex also provides personalized training looks, smart pacing guidance based on where you're at, automatically adjusting incline for classes, and of course leaderboards and an entire ecosystem of badges and achievements to earn, if you're into all that. For $50 per year, that is.

Oh, and did I mention it's a good-looking machine? It's sleek; an attractive, soft-edged Z with a minimal screen instead of a board of colorful buttons. Nobody's throwing around the word "console" to describe this thing. That's good; home gym setups deserve different consideration than gym rigs. If images of Crunch Fitness flash through your head every time you glance into the corner, something has missed the mark.

Where Peloton's Tread Vision treadmills are clearly high-end, the Tread Flex toes the line against mainstream consumer models. Its features match up with some of the most popular machines, and its price, while at the higher end of the spectrum, does too. But the Tread Flex gets there with more style, and with Peloton's huge ecosystem of live and archived class content.

Sources indicate that so, if we're looking at other treadmills out there, my quick answer is yes. The Tread Flex is the utilitarian Peloton Treadmill, but it's still a Peloton treadmill.

Recent findings suggest that how you answer this question really requires asking yourself a series of other questions first. What do you want a treadmill for? How much do you want to invest? Do you want access to fitness classes—especially ones other than running—and are you okay with the $50/month subscription fee?

Industry observers note that form factor and access to classes and content are non-negotiables. The Tread Flex might be Peloton's upcoming entry-level treadmill, but it's far from a simple running machine. Flex refers to that nifty fold-up feature, but also to this treadmill's ability to integrate into an exercise program that also includes strength training, HIIT workouts, yoga, and on and on.

Sources indicate that as a runner who prefers to log miles outside whenever possible, I was encouraged by how much I enjoyed running on the Tread Flex. The classes are fun, and Peloton's instructors are real pros, but even in Just Run mode, the Tread Flex proved responsive and comfy. It's getting dark around 4:30 PM these days, and my daylight windows for running on the well-used roads around me have narrowed like a Death Star trash compactor. It's nice to know I can snag seven miles after sundown if need be.

According to recent reports, well, if you aren't limited by space or cash, the Tread Vision and Tread+ Vision get you bigger screens, AI-enabled running form feedback and coaching, and a more cushioned, broader running area. If you just prefer running or walking on a treadmill to doing it outside, investing more heavily in a treadmill is worth considering (though the Tread Flex will still be great).

The Tread Flex's real competition is the NordicTrack Commercial 1750, which you'll find recommended on just about every treadmill buying guide on the internet. The machines are similar in function and specs, but there are some differences. The NordicTrack's running surface is two inches wider and one inch longer; it has a slightly more powerful motor; it can decline to -3% grade; its belt is slightly cushioned; it has a built-in fan; and NordicTrack's class and entertainment platform, iFit, is cheaper at $39 a month.

In comparison, the Tread Flex takes up slightly less space, has a higher max speed (12.5 mph over 12 mph), a steeper incline (12.5% over 12%), and a larger screen (21.5 inches over 16 inches). The rolling knobs to adjust speed and incline are nicer to use. My partner, who designs commercial and residential interior spaces, agrees with me that the Tread Flex is a better-looking machine.

List price for the Tread Flex is $300 cheaper, but the NordicTrack seems to be perpetually on sale. So it might come down to looks, that 3% decline, or what class platform you'd like to buy into.

From the red-carpet heavy-hitters to Hollywood’s next generation of stars and the stylists making it all happen, the honorees on our 2026 best-dressed list all share a love for a great outfit. It certainly helps that we do too—which is why we’re coming in with the cold, hard facts: We’re breaking down their style signifiers, one shoppable piece at a time.

The names on this year’s list range from celebrity street style regulars—see: Jennifer Lawrence—to relative newcomers like actor Sarah Pidgeon and singer Gracie Abrams. Model and CFDA judge Paloma Elsesser and actor Ayo Edebiri both appear for their second year in a row on Vogue’s Best Dressed list.

Ahead, you’ll have the chance to browse through some of the honorees’ best looks of 2026, with a snapshot of the key pieces that made those outfits stand out to us—and in turn, dominate the sartorial conversation at Vogue HQ. Some stars championed CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund nominees early on: Edebiri and Lee both wore Lii for press appearances this year, while Lawrence sported one of Colleen Allen’s velvet house coats with a white tee and slippers on a mild fall day in New York. Others are vintage fiends at heart—Elsesser, who self-styled her Vogue Shopping cover shoot in September—chief among them; her everyday looks comprise a mix of vintage Junya Watanabe and Comme des Garçons and emerging designers.

Below, a snapshot of the wardrobes that make up Vogue’s Best Dressed list of 2026, complete with the key pieces needed to shop their signature looks and make them your own.

In a recent development, A regular fixture in our weekly celeb outfits roundups, Jennifer Lawrence is known for her effortless brand of messy-chic, cool-mom-at-drop-off looks, often centered around a ball cap and a slubby vintage tee. The Row and Khaite are mainstay labels in rotation, though, let the record show that she loves mixing more eclectic pieces—like her Colleen Allen velvet house coat—with simple basics (Leset is noted a go-to).

In a recent development, sarah Pidgeon’s debut on Vogue’s Best Dressed List comes as no surprise: Since playing the role of ’90s style icon, Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy on Ryan Murphy’s Love Story, Pidgeon has taken method acting to a fresh level with method dressing. For the majority of her public appearances, Pidgeon has stepped out in pieces reflective of Bessette-Kennedy’s refrained style, like a Yohji Yamamoto dress, a collarless Aflalo leather trench, and an embellished mint green slip from Chanel.

Model and CFDA judge Paloma Elsesser is a modern cool-girl, known for her IYKYK approach to dressing . A champion of emerging designers like the London-based, Central Saint Martins graduate Goyagoma, her eclectic style is typically supplemented by vintage grails from the likes Junya Watanabe and Comme des Garçons. For those who worship at the altar of “quiet luxury,” Elsesser eschews that with bold prints, vivid color, and a style that’s all her own.

Like her repertoire of acting roles (TV: The Bear, film: Clarissa, Broadway: Proof), Ayo Edebiri’s style shows as much range as her career choices—from repping emerging designers like Giovanna Flores in a patchwork dress to Conner Ives in pinstripe suiting (yes, the same Ives whose fur-trimmed coat just broke the internet), to her more mature choices for the red carpet, such as Chanel and The Row. Edebiri doesn’t limit herself to one style or silhouette—she can go from feminine dressing to masculine suiting, just as easily as she can shift into various characters (Pacino, anyone?).

Known for her starring roles in this year’s Toy Story 5, as well as in Tron: Ares, and Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, actor Greta Lee’s sartorial choices take a page out of her action-flick lineup, albeit, with a fashion-forward twist. A fan of bold color-blocking, Lee has worn CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund winner Lii, as well as a fire-engine red fringed gown by High Sport to the London premiere of Toy Story 5, while making bold fashion choices with Marc Jacobs’s iconic blue sequin strapless top from the spring 2026 collection.

It has been revealed that it’s been a banner year for the actress Carey Mulligan—in March, she accepted a royal honor in the form of a CBE (Commander of the Order of the British Empire) from King Charles III for her services to drama. Even at Windsor Castle, she used the opportunity to show up in a royally-fashionable ensemble (one, we might say, was fit for a king!) wearing a jacket and trousers from The Row, accessorized with Jacques Marie Mage sunglasses. Then, for the season two premiere of Beef in which she plays a starring role, Mulligan showed up in a pixelated floral skirt and brocade bustier top from designer Julian Klausner’s fall 2026 collection for Dries Van Noten. Her red carpet looks are a mix of sumptuous color, pattern, and texture, illustrated best in a full Colleen Allen look composed of a ruffled velvet top with a coordinating silk column skirt in sunburnt orange.

Another one in Lii’s fashionable girl-gang, actor Whitney Peak (who stars as Lenore Dove Baird in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping) appreciates a color-blocked ensemble, whether it’s for a magazine launch or a press appearance (the latter saw her in London-based designer Torishéju). Her color palettes skews minimalist—think neutrals punctuated by flashes of red—but the silhouettes she gravitates towards are anything but. Case in point: the knitted black Diotima dress she wore to the Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles was a maximalist’s dream.

It has been revealed that actor Tessa Thompson has been delivering on the red carpet for years now — and her style only continues to bring the wow-factor, from being a fellow fan of Giovanna Flores’s patchwork dress to Kallmeyer’s tailored suiting. She’s known to love a sharp, structured shoulder, and has a penchant for contrasting a delicate silk dress with a strong leather jacket paired. With her Golden Globes nomination for Hedda, starring in the Netflix thriller His & Hers, and a Broadway debut in Fear of 13, co-starring Adrien Brody, Thompson’s style is one that delivers as much variety and star power as her resume.

Our mother in style, Tracee Ellis Ross’s wardrobe is as bright as her star power. With this year’s Broadway debut in Every Brilliant Thing and a daytime Emmy for her show, Solo Traveling, she stepped up her style game even further, with the help of her stylist Law Roach. The Girlfriends and Black-ish star has been experimenting with color and texture as of late, stepping out in highly-saturated ensembles that span an embellished Prada skirt and button-down (look 22 from the fall runway), a marigold tasseled gown by Balenciaga (designed by Pierpaolo Piccioli for spring 2027), and punchy Dries Van Noten (look 35, also from SS27).

Recent findings suggest that after returning to the stage this year with a 16-show sold out residency at Paris’s Plénitude Arena, Celine Dion delivered what the people wanted—and so much more. With daily paparazzi shots that highlighted off her good humor in style, she stepped out in looks that ranged from suede Jacquemus to all-black leather Tom Ford. Quintessential French design, in feather-trimmed Dior and custom Chanel (she wore a gown that was recreation of her 1997 Oscars dress) rounded out this Canadian in Paris’s sojourn.

Industry observers note that the former First Lady has been having fun with fashion as of late—donning a Thom Browne suit set for a ribbon-cutting at the Barack Obama Presidential Center one day to a custom Acne Studios skirt printed with a photo of her late mother, Marian Robinson, the next. At the US Open this summer, she wore a red, white, and navy blue striped Chanel dress from the resort 2027 collection.

According to recent reports, ever since the 2026 CFDA Fashion Awards, we haven’t been able to get Gracie Abrams as a gothic vision in Colleen Allen out of our minds. The singer has been serving looks long before that though, stepping out in her signature mix of vintage tees, Conner Ives rugby polos and trousers, and an enviable collection of Chanel pumps. Equal parts comfy and stylish, she’s known to wear a quirky mashup of styles and designers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Michelle Yeoh has spent decades bringing stories to the silver screen—with roles in hit films like Crazy Rich Asians and Wicked to the upcoming Blade Runner 2099—but her love life has a pretty remarkable story of its own.

The Oscar-winning actress married French businessman and former Ferrari CEO Jean Todt in 2023, nearly 19 years after he first proposed. The pair have been together since 2004, supporting each other through career milestones, international travels, and plenty of memorable moments along the way. But who is the man standing by one of Hollywood’s most accomplished actresses?

Ahead, everything you need to know about Yeoh’s husband, Jean Todt, including his career in motorsports, how the couple met, and their long-awaited wedding.

In a recent development, todt was born on February 25, 1946, in Pierrefort, a commune in France’s South-Central region. He studied at École des Cadres School of Economics and Business in Paris. At 80 years old, he’s 16 years Yeoh’s senior.

Industry observers note that todt is best known for his work in motorsports, but his career actually began behind the wheel—or, more accurately, in the passenger seat. He started as a rally co-driver, a role he held from 1966 to 1981, before moving into the business and management side of racing.

From there, he went on to work with some of the biggest names in the industry. In 1981, he joined Peugeot as its director of racing before founding Peugeot Talbot Sport, where he helped the team secure multiple World Rally Championship titles. In 1993, he moved to Ferrari, eventually becoming the firm’s general manager in 2004 and CEO in 2006, a position he held until 2008.

But his career didn’t end with Ferrari. In 2009, Todt was elected president of the Fédération Internationale de l’Automobile (FIA), the governing body for international motorsports, including Formula One. He held the position for 12 years, until 2021, and has also served as the United Nations secretary general's special envoy for road safety since 2015.

In a recent development, yeoh and Todt’s love story began in Shanghai, China, in June 2004. Yeoh attended a Ferrari event, where she met Todt, who was then the company’s general manager. According to the couple’s wedding program, they first crossed paths on June 4, 2004, and Todt proposed less than two months later, on July 26. Yeoh said yes, beginning what would become a nearly two-decade engagement.

After nearly 19 years together, Yeoh and Todt finally tied the knot on July 27, 2023, in Geneva, Switzerland, surrounded by family and friends. Brazilian racing driver Felipe Massa first shared the news, posting photos from the celebration on social media. Todt later confirmed the marriage and called Yeoh the love of his life.

The couple’s wedding program included a sweet recap of their relationship, noting that they had met 6,992 days earlier. Yeoh also shared photos from the celebration on Instagram, writing, “19 years and YES!! we are married!!” The actress wore several looks for the occasion, including a champagne-colored gown, and celebrated with loved ones—including her upcoming husband’s colleagues from the world of Formula One.

Todt has one son, Nicolas, from a previous relationship. Born on November 17, 1977, Nicolas has followed in his father’s footsteps, carving out his own career in motorsports. He is a racing manager and talent manager who has worked with some of the sport’s biggest names, including Charles Leclerc and Felipe Massa.

Sticky Miso Chicken and More Recipes We Made This Week

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1473 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work.
  • My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking.
  • Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here.

My husband and I recently took our 3-year-old daughter apple picking. As expected at the tail end of the season, the only apples left were Granny Smith. A perfect apple for baking, I decided to peruse our new app to see what fit the bill and found Zaynab Issa’s Caramel Apple Snacking Cake. After scanning the instructions, it seemed like a fairly straightforward one-bowl situation—the perfect pace for my lazy Sunday. I grated the apples right into a large bowl, and mixed it with the dry and wet ingredients before baking. The cake is elevated with a quick caramel that gets drizzled on top, which makes it feel fancy. —June Kim, executive editor.

Armed with a fresh trio of cumin, coriander, and turmeric from Diaspora Spice Co., I decided to make Alison Roman’s Chicken Tikka Masala. It’s a bit of a project, but the payoff is worth it. The spice-rich sauce takes 30 to 40 minutes, but let it go closer to 40 for something thick, concentrated, and luxurious. Broiling is a genius move: Set on a wire rack, the yogurt-marinated chicken gets air on all sides, so it blackens instead of steaming before being added to the sauce. To accompany the main, we made a side of Priya Krishna’s Aloo Gobi in the air fryer. It came out crispy and caramelized, at least until I coated it in the creamy sauce. —Olivia Tarantino, senior shopping editor.

According to recent reports, with a name like Just-Keeps-Getting-Better Lentil Salad, how could you go wrong? My former colleague Sarah Jampel’s rightfully beloved recipe is one of those staples I’ve made so many times, I don’t even need to look at it to double-check quantities or instructions anymore. It’s become second nature. And when I’m feeling inspired, or my pantry has seen better days, it’s pretty adaptable too. This week I whipped up a huge bowl with walnuts and cashews in place of the almonds, a blood orange standing in for the lemon, and added some lovely chicories to mingle with the kale. As always, it was crunchy and fresh, tender and filling, even three days after I whipped it up. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

Sources indicate that I love cookbook author Samantha Seneviratne’s recipes and her recent one for a tahini cake crusted with sesame seeds called to me. Just the thing for a fall weekend. I scaled down the recipe for my 8x8" pan using Kendra Vaculin’s handy conversion guide. And I did a mix of white and black sesame seeds on top for fun. It was plush and not too sweet—great for dessert and even better for breakfast the next day. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

I’ve been holding on to this recipe for years, and it’s finally time I release it into the world. Be free Sticky Miso Chicken! It’s made with a three-ingredient marinade with stuff you probably already have in your cupboard. Equal parts miso and honey, plus a healthy splash of soy sauce mixed together creates a million-dollar burnished glaze. I slather the marinade onto chicken thighs, but you could also do chicken breast, salmon, shrimp, tofu. Go wild. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Every fall I stuff my pantry with cans of pumpkin purée. And fortunately our annual Pumpkin Week tells me exactly what to do with the haul. I’m always in search of more savory uses for the ingredient, and my coworker Jesse Szewczyk’s Pumpkin Black Bean Enchiladas were right up my alley. I did a mix of black and kidney beans (what was around) and I toned down the spice for my toddler who—the universe laughs—refused to eat them anyway, instead opting to smear the sauce all over his clothes. C’est la vie! —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Industry observers note that there is a latest vendor at my greenmarket who makes incredible buffalo milk yogurt. My favorite is flavored with tangy, floral passion fruit. It’s not too sweet and works beautifully with fruit and granola. To showcase its power as a sauce, I made David Tamarkin’s apple olive oil cake (baked in an 8" round instead of a loaf) and served the yogurt underneath. For the cake, you shred a couple of apples then squeeze out their juices, which you can then drink for a baker’s treat. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite things is to use a banana bread recipe to make muffins and call it meal prep. I pack this gluten-free batter into tins, sprinkle on some flaxseed and pecans, and reduce the bake time. They can easily pass for breakfast, an afternoon snack, or dessert, and the recipe yields enough muffins to be enjoyed throughout the week with a scoop of yogurt or swipe of nut butter. —Kate Kassin, editorial operations manager.

Sources indicate that with a recipe entitled Bob’s Chicken and Cabbage Salad, I’m sure you’re wondering: Who the heck is Bob? Author Melissa Broder’s late father, who happened to be fervently devoted to purple cabbage. Well, Bob, me too—especially after trying this one. Per the instructions, I chopped up half a head of cabbage, baby bok choy, scallions, bean sprouts, and water chestnuts, then tossed the roughage with pulled chicken. This time around, I did cheat with a store-bought rotisserie bird to jump-start cooking (it was 8 p.m. when I started, okay?). That also meant halving the heavenly soy-ginger dressing, since I no longer needed some of it for the marinade. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

Sources indicate that my Test Kitchen buddy Rebecca Firkser has a wild little pasta up her sleeve that I can’t get enough of: Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates. When she first made it for the team, I was blown away. I would have never thought to throw dates into a pasta, but alas, it’s delicious. Each bite has something sweet, something creamy, a bit of crunch, and endless fun. —Jesse Szewczyk, senior Test Kitchen editor.

It has been revealed that since my son started daycare in September, our household has been sick more than it has been healthy. So it makes sense that I have been on a chicken soup kick. I have it for lunch and dinner and drink mugfuls of stock between meals. My latest batch was my colleague Rebecca Firkser’s Toasted Orzo Chicken Soup, which has a beautifully spiced broth and lots of nourishing spinach. It may not be a cure-all, but close enough. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director.

Delicata squash should be as popular as butternut. It’s far easier to cut (no hacks or hacking necessary), the thin skin is not only edible but tasty, and it’s got a sweet potato-like flesh that’s creamy and, well, sweet. I usually treat it simply (oil, salt and pepper, hot oven, done), but I treated myself to my former colleague Rachel Gurjar’s gussied-up Roasted Delicata Squash With Crispy Onions and I’m so glad I did. The squash itself takes no extra effort, but gathering up some toppings, like store-bought fried onions tossed with extra spices, juicy pomegranate seeds, and seasoned yogurt, transformed it into a dish I was proud to serve to guests. —Kelsey Jane Youngman, senior cooking editor.

It has been revealed that we have a fresh Friday tradition at our house: Pasta Alla Vodka and Caesar salad. Not rocket science, I know, but after a rough-and-tumble week of work and school, we are all reaching for some semblance of comfort. It is also easy enough to whip up that I can often beat the timing of our former Friday tradition, take-out pizza. The Caesar dressing is usually made in advance (I keep a batch in the fridge because my family lurves it) and the pasta of choice is usually rigatoni. It cooks in about the same amount of time as the sauce—I just love when that happens. —Hana Asbrink, deputy food editor.

It has been revealed that there’s nothing more perfect than a tuna melt. Buttery slices of sourdough or rye that leave a shine of grease on your fingers. Tuna salad mashed into tender flakes, speckled with crisp celery, onion, and herbs. A blanket of American cheese, so stretchy it’ll rival a mozzarella stick. And a mandatory pickle, to offer added tangy solace after each bite. I ate mine with salt-and-vinegar kettle chips stuffed inside because that’s how my favorite diner does it. —Nina Moskowitz, associate editor, cooking.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s a glorious late-September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me.
  • Industry observers note that still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me.
  • In a recent development, he speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s a glorious late-September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me. A soft breeze hints at the seasonal shift that will soon blanket this bucolic corner of Utah in frost. I’m standing beside two of Daniel Neeleman’s daughters and Daniel himself, his head full of curly hair and his feet tucked into work boots. He exudes the easy familiarity of an old friend, despite a family name—and now a social media presence, thanks to Ballerina Farm’s 20 million–plus combined followers—that has taken on a life of its own.

Industry observers note that still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me. “We love small agriculture and the diversification of it,” he states. “I think that we can make an impact in helping people see that small agriculture can work. Whether you’re doing an agritourism aspect or not, we still think it should and can be profitable.”.

In a recent development, he speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America. Daniel did not grow up with animals and still remembers how mesmerized he was the first time he saw a cow. “I tell people on the farm tours all the time, if your endorphins are going off watching these animals, watch out. You might be a farmer. It doesn’t go away—it might come back to you later in life.” From the very day that Daniel and his now famous wife, Hannah, bought their first farm in 2017, he knew this was where they were meant to be.

According to recent reports, earlier that morning, I was sitting at their kitchen dining table over a brunch of quiche, greens, yogurt, and tea made from just-picked mint, the spread illuminated by beeswax spindle candles. “It’s our responsibility, and our love and passion too, to build this,” Hannah tells me, wearing a white dress with three daughters by her side. She’s sitting against a backdrop that’s become familiar to millions who have watched her cook and feed her growing family on a farm less than an hour outside Salt Lake City.

Recent findings suggest that despite their sincere intentions, the Neelemans’ endeavor has brought moments of global controversy. The internet has scrutinized their approach to homeschooling their nine children, their family wealth, and how they balance their roles as parents and cofounders. “We don’t take the platform that we’ve been given lightly,” Hannah says. Agriculture, she explains, has been at the heart of the project from the beginning, even as its reach has expanded far beyond the Kamas Valley. “It has worn a lot of different hats as it’s grown. We were young city kids, and we craved something real and knowing where our food comes from.”.

According to recent reports, now, what began as a story told online is becoming a universe people can actually step into. On a stretch of land that spreads out beyond the window like something from “America the Beautiful,” they’re planning—and here announcing—one of the country’s most ambitious fresh farm hospitality destinations: a cookery school, farm-to-table restaurant, farm store, and spaces for agricultural education and events, all set within a working farm encompassing livestock, organic gardens, a dairy, and a forthcoming creamery.

According to recent reports, at the heart of the vision is a cookery school, scheduled to open in 2029, that is as much about learning to cook from the farm as it is about taking those lessons home. The goal is to teach people how to cook seasonally and adapt when certain ingredients aren’t available, wherever they might live. (Daniel describes this as an education in life skills rather than formal chef training.) “I want students to have time with the dairy, the market garden, the creamery, so they’re seeing where the food comes from,” Hannah notes.

The cookery school will be guided by a philosophy similar to that of the legendary Ballymaloe Cookery School, where Hannah and Daniel spent 12 weeks in 2025—and first met Michael “Tiffin” Griffin, a beloved longtime instructor who has since joined Ballerina Farm as the director of the culinary experience. (A more formal, fine-dining restaurant may eventually complement the school.).

But visitors can step into the new Ballerina Farm world as soon as fall 2027, when a Dutch barn is slated to open at the site of the current Kamas market. Inside will be a restaurant and café, which the couple collectively calls an “eatery,” serving meals featuring the meat, dairy, and produce grown on the surrounding farm—a considerable expansion of the current menus at the Midway store and food truck.

Across a breezeway, a market will offer fresh produce straight from the garden and meat and dairy from the livestock—think onions, pea shoots, beets, rib-eye steaks, smoked paprika goat cheese, and gallons of A2/A2 cream-top whole milk—as well as a growing selection of prepared sides, sauces, and meals, from pickled torpedo onions to just-juiced turmeric ginger shots to chicken salad. The latter is Hannah’s particular favorite. “We got so attached to the chicken salad that we had this summer, because we grew meat chickens. We harvested them. And they made the most delicious chicken salad. Then Tiffin told us this week, ‘One more week of the chicken salad—I’m out of pickles. You’ll see it next spring.’ And I went, ‘Nooo.’” She laughs. “I think people are getting back to how grandma used to cook. She cooked from the garden, and it was amazing food.”.

Just-cut spinach and radishes will sit next to Ballerina Farm’s signature products, initially available only online, as well as Ballerina Farm’s home goods like oven mitts, aprons, and wooden measuring spoons, with the name appearing only discreetly. They also launched their first skin-care product just this month: Tallow Tin body butter—made with tallow from the cattle, naturally.

Sources indicate that the restaurant, farm store, and connecting courtyard will be more than five times the size of the existing Ballerina Farm store and café that opened in 2025, 25 minutes down the road in Midway. “There’s an awful lot of hullabaloo about Hannah doing it, but for me that’s what I saw when I was a kid,” Tiffin, the culinary director, tells me. “That’s how my grandmother lived her life.”.

Over a two-hour meal of Ballerina Farm roasted chicken, garden carrots, pickled onions, and homemade yogurt, I sat enraptured by Tiffin’s story and the depth of knowledge and experience that had brought him to this particular farm in Utah. While guests can expect a diversity of dishes—Tiffin is especially passionate about Moroccan flavors—the land is the final decision maker. “We’ll ask Tiffin what’s on the menu for an event,” Daniel explains, “and the first thing he’ll say is, ‘Let me call Madison [Goodman], the head grower.’”.

In a recent development, goodman is responsible for a vegetable operation that will eventually expand to five acres. The kitchen will draw on its harvest but supplement it with neighboring producers when necessary—a philosophy similar to that which guided Tiffin at Ballymaloe: “If we can’t grow it, we get it locally. If we can’t get it locally, we’ll get the best.”.

It has been revealed that the design and architecture of the project, meanwhile, will be led by Patrick Williams of Berdoulat, the British design house known for its richly textured, historically informed interiors. At Berdoulat, the mantra is “the house rules.” But as Williams puts it, “In this instance, where the buildings are yet to exist, the land rules.” His designs draw inspiration from 19th-century settlers’ homes and agricultural buildings in the Kamas Valley (and, yes, the family’s famous farmstead).

The Ballerina Farm team has worked closely with Kamas officials for years now to define what can be developed on its 14-acre property, prompting the city to introduce upcoming agritourism zoning in 2024. The looks also protect the property’s conserved wetlands. “We are constantly in touch with the city,” says Brad Roberts, the brand’s director of marketing. If done well, Kamas can become a role model for the many other small towns grappling with their own decisions around the opportunities made possible through agritourism.

Sources indicate that yet the Kamas Valley is not the most obvious place to craft such an ambitious project that’s certain to draw travelers not only from the coasts but also from overseas. (Eighty percent of Ballerina Farm’s 10 million–plus Instagram following is based outside of the US.) A high water table can flood the gardens, frosts set in as early as October, and voles relentlessly try to work their way into the harvest. But the valley has a certain quality of light, giant skies, and an openness that feels rarer than ever in today’s world.

In a recent development, walking through three high tunnels filled to the brim with produce, I eventually met Goodman, a fourth-generation farmer who ran his own successful community-supported agriculture program in the Kamas Valley and was courted for years by the Neelemans before joining the Ballerina Farm team. He speaks passionately about the farm’s recently earned USDA organic certification and the decades of advocacy that brought those standards into existence. “You can make me cry, because there are a lot of people who fought hard for this,” Goodman states, describing the certification’s baseline standards as the floor while emphasizing that he’s reaching for the ceiling. “The label helps us bridge this gap that we, as a society, have created between our reality.”.

He continues: “Everything here has a story. I can tell you the story of the winter leek. I can tell you the story of these girls.” (The girls are chickens.) He then spends 10 minutes explaining to me exactly why these chickens—Freedom Rangers rather than the more commonly raised Cornish Cross—are so special and how they’re raised from chicks to harvest. “It’s hard for me to do this and not believe in a creator,” Goodman says.

One of the challenges and opportunities of an agritourism project is that, in a four-season destination like Utah, the experience will be remarkably different depending on when visitors arrive: tomatoes in the summer, spinach in the winter, chicks in one season, and a mature flock in another. “There’s something beautiful about eating what’s in season and retraining us as eaters to appreciate that,” Hannah reflects. “I have started to notice that I’m craving spinach, pumpkin, and squash because your body wants the things that are growing.”.

The culture side of agriculture has probably played a larger role in the Neelemans’ agricultural pursuits than they expected, however. While Hannah started sharing on social media as a way to kick-start business for their nascent pork operation, it snowballed into a public inquisition over what many perceived as an idealized, regressive performance of rural domesticity. But what the public wanted to know most was how it was possible. What was real? And who funded it?

Industry observers note that when I ask them about balancing their ambitious vision with the realities of building a farm and business, Hannah claims, “That’s a true founder of a firm. They are the one who has to hold those two worlds together. We have to keep the dreams alive and the fire burning, but we’re also camping over the farm stand or dealing with broken pipes and trying to put up hoop houses.”.

Industry observers note that daniel adds: “We’re the ones that decide whenever there’s money left over at the end of the month from the business.” He says that every individual part of the business is profitable. “We don’t have any investors, we don’t have any partners—it’s just us. So then it’s just a question of, What projects are we going to conquer first? We are a for-profit company, and we have to be good stewards of the finances of all the things. It has to be sustainable.”.

For years, people have been asking to visit, Hannah explains, sending her messages asking to meet the animals, help with chores, or simply spend a day on the farm. At the time, the Neelemans weren’t equipped to receive this audience of millions who had developed a relationship with a place they’d never visited. Now, they’re preparing to welcome both admirers and curious outsiders, as well as farmers and cooks, into the world that has generated so much conversation. “We have a community that wants to be a part of it,” Hannah recalls thinking. “So how do we build it?”.

This new expression of Ballerina Farm places Hannah and Daniel among a lineage of visionaries in farm hospitality who have transformed working farms into gathering places—Ballymaloe, yes, but also Daylesford Organic in the English Cotswolds and Babylonstoren in South Africa. But of course, one crucial factor sets Ballerina Farm’s journey apart. Rather than building a hospitality destination and then finding an audience, the Neelemans are working the other way around. The relationship is already shaped by years of watching the family’s life unfold online—and by the very different ideas people have formed about what Ballerina Farm represents.

Sources indicate that it’s easy to understand the appeal: Rather than watch a 60-second video on their phones, visitors can pull sourdough or slip on a Ballerina Farm oven mitt and slide a pork chop out of the oven. They can greet a just-born calf. Their children can run the fields, breathe the fresh Utah air, and taste the milk from Daniel’s cows. As I pulled through the gates of Ballerina Farm in my rental car and watched six Sebastopol geese waddle in front of me, even I felt that very modern feeling of disorienting familiarity upon experiencing a person or a place in the flesh that I had only ever seen on a screen.

In a recent development, right now, the Kamas property has already begun hosting farm dinners, seasonal events, and agricultural experiences alongside the market and food truck. Each offering showcases how the Ballerina Farm world will eventually come together: market, meals, events, education, animals, and gardens all in one place.

It has been revealed that and for all the ambition of what Hannah and Daniel are building, the idea at its heart remains deeply personal. “The greatest work that we can do is in our homes and our own families and our communities,” Hannah tells me, a conviction that has remained constant even as Ballerina Farm’s audience has rapidly grown.

Adds Daniel, “We’ve accomplished some things that we’re proud of, but we’re far from being done.”.

The most recent version required interested collectors to fill out an “Electronic Swatch Timepiece Application” in hopes of being selected to purchase one. More than 1.2 million people happily played along. Now, Swatch and Omega are back and playing the hits with a Snoopy-inflected version of the MoonSwatch.

Meet the new Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake. The blacked-out watch is reminiscent of the collector-favorite Speedmaster known as the “Dark Side of the Moon” from 2013. What that watch was lacking compared to this one is an adorable drawing of Snoopy and Woodstock dressed as astronauts and a special silver disc with a unique laser-engraved snowflake design. Safe to say, Omega and Swatch have another hit on their hands.

Industry observers note that the black-on-black-on-black design works to great effect here. Everything is rendered in the dark shade: the case, bezel, dial, and matching rubber strap with Velcro closure. Like all MoonSwatch references, the Silver Snowflake model measures 42mm in diameter and features the asymmetric design familiar to Speedy lovers everywhere.

But it’s the easter eggs on the dial that really make this MoonSwatch stand out. Naturally, there are several hidden details. For instance, check out the miniature skis standing in for the indices at 11 o'clock. That’s a special shoutout to the Apollo 11 50th Anniversary of the Speedmaster. This model also returns to a trick employed by the “Cold Moon” MoonSwatch released last November. That watch and this one feature a snowflake design generated at random, meaning each watch is functionally unique. Here, the snowflake appears on a silver-coated disc in the moonphase complication at 2 o’clock.

Industry observers note that at 10 o’clock is Swatch and Omega’s signature MoonSwatch “Earth phase” indicator, which bears an image of the Earth with UV ink-coated oceans set against a starry background. Again, look closely: Switzerland is represented in white, its UV ink glowing green in the dark, while Snoopy and Woodstock, represented below, feature secret details in blue-emission UV ink. Protecting the dial is a box-shaped, bio-sourced crystal with an engraved “S” in the center—a detail familiar to fans of vintage Speedmasters, some of which bore “O”-engraved Hesalite crystals.

Sources indicate that like several other MoonSwatch models in the brand’s now-vast collection, buying the Mission to Earthphase - Silver Snowflake requires navigating certain arcane rules. The first part is simple: it’ll be available in stores worldwide this Black Friday, November 27th. However, following that, your only chance to nab one will be when it’s snowing in Switzerland. (And only until March 20th, 2027.) When it comes to the MoonSwatch, simply buying one has become half the fun.
